extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on structuring and writing accident stories and covering court news: how to order information, use background and dialogue, and explain legal procedures clearly for general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block structure for accident stories (primary arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Block 1: Usually one paragraph; summary of all the accidents with the lead accident mentioned first. Block 2: As many paragraphs as called for; details of the lead accident. Block 3: As long as may be needed; details of the lesser accidents, in the order of mention in Block 1. Block 4: As many paragraphs as needed; details of the other accidents, in the same order as their mention in Block 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this four-block arrangement to organize casualty lists and detailed accounts; follow the order of mention in the summary when expanding details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative block arrangement for accident stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The other arrangement is: Block 1: Usually one paragraph; summary of all the accidents with the lead accident mentioned first. Block 2: As many paragraphs as called for; details of the lead accident. Block 3: As long as may be needed; details of the lesser accidents, in the order of mention in Block 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variation compresses or omits a separately numbered 'Block 4' — if Block 1 hasn't mentioned specific mishaps, detail lesser mishaps in order of descending interest rather than strict lead-paragraph sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casualty list placement in accident stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The casualty list (summary of persons killed or injured) should be in the lead or immediately after the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place casualty list high in the story so readers quickly learn who was hurt; when producing second-day accounts include a concise tie-in to the original casualty list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-background and later-background split
rubrics_metrics.description: If background can be handled briefly, it is often run immediately after the casualty list; if background cannot be cut down so much, it is split — a 'lead background' following the casualty list and the details of the background coming at the end of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When background is long, consider printing it as a separate adjoining story. Use the split method to keep the lead tight while preserving necessary context later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialog and 'flashes' to make accident stories interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the accident story interesting is principally a matter of finding out its details. A flash or two of dialog often will do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring forward short quoted dialogue or vivid moments to give the story 'breath of life.' The example contrasts a direct quote with a diluted paraphrase to show impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer vivid direct quotes to diluted paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotes have 'the breath of life'; paraphrased versions are lusterless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, publish striking first-person dialog from witnesses (e.g., 'I didn't know where the devil I was going') rather than bland third-person paraphrase; even short flashes of dialog strengthen a short story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring forward interesting sidelight details
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of no importance that this fire is the third successive blaze at which Hoseman Joe Bailey has been injured, but this sidelight makes the story more authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include apparently small but revealing facts that show the reporter 'dug deep' and that add authority and interest, especially in short pieces where chosen words are distilled from much larger reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés in accident reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The cliché does more than any other factor to make accident stories deadly alike; avoid stock phrases like 'narrow escape', 'belching smoke', 'angry waters', and imprecise labels like calling any derailment a 'crack' train.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent fresh, precise descriptions; steer clear of bromides and current journalistic fads that trivialize or flatten the scene. The example lampoons overused terms and urges editors to correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering lesser mishaps by descending interest when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Block 1 has not mentioned specifically any of the other mishaps, their later detailing can be in the order of descending interest rather than in any lead-paragraph sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the summary is general, arrange subsequent details to maximize reader interest, not strictly to match the initial listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-day story tie-in placement and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: This tie-in usually follows immediately after the lead and is placed high in the story for the benefit of readers who missed the first-day news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-day incidents, begin follow-up articles with a succinct recap (lead tie-in) of the original story so newcomers are brought up to date; keep it short and high in the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortening the tie-in over successive days
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer the story lives, the shorter the tie-in can be, until finally it is only a subordinate clause spliced deftly into the lead paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce repetition across days but be careful not to excise essential earlier facts or angles; compress recaps as reader familiarity increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not drop important earlier angles in follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: A follow story that omitted mention of a previously prominent aspect (e.g., sabotage) misleads readers who missed earlier stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain mention of central earlier developments (like suspected sabotage) in follow-ups so that readers who missed initial coverage still grasp the significant angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use background to explain series or distinctive elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Background is largely an explaining that this new accident is one of a series or that it has certain distinctive elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background sparingly when it clarifies pattern or distinctiveness; if lengthy, split it or make it a separate story to avoid bogging the main narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate legal minutiae for readers without losing significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing legal minutiae is perpetually hard, for they must be translated so that readers who know or understand neither mittimus nor mandamus can comprehend. He must make this simplification without losing the shades of significance which may decide a case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain technical legal terms and procedures in plain English but preserve the nuances that affect outcomes; balance simplification with accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain statutory vs common (case) law and jurisdictional reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Law splits into statutory (officially enacted) and common (decisions and rulings made by judges) law; statutory law applies at the level that enacted it, common law arises from established practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting, indicate whether an issue derives from statute or case law and clarify the territorial or institutional reach (city, state, national) so readers understand scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish criminal and civil law and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal law concerns acts against 'the people' and carries punishment; civil law concerns individual disputes and seeks relief such as damages or equity remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear whether a story involves criminal prosecution (punishment) or civil remedies (money, injunctions) and explain the practical differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report arrest authority and warrant distinctions (felony vs misdemeanor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone can arrest a person suspected of a felony at any time; for misdemeanors, arrest must usually occur while the offense is taking place unless authorized by a warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering arrests, state whether they were warrantless and on what legal basis; explain the misdemeanor/felony distinctions relevant to the arrest's legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain warrants, bench warrants, informations, and complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: A warrant is a written order issued after a sworn complaint. A bench warrant follows indictment or information. An information is a sworn complaint by the state's attorney; a complaint is a sworn accusation by a private citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify for readers which procedural vehicle led to custody or charges and what that implies about the stage and seriousness of the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain grand jury role and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A grand jury hears purported evidence in secret and decides whether accusations are substantial enough to justify trial; it acts only in felonies and its action is not a finding of guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report grand-jury actions (indictment or no-bill) and stress that indictment is a step to trial, not proof of guilt; note states that have abolished grand juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey the accused's two opportunities for exoneration (preliminary hearing and trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The preliminary hearing (or grand jury) may drop the case; if not, the accused has a second chance to obtain exoneration by trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the purpose of preliminary hearings and bail determinations so readers understand stages and protections afforded the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe trial procedure clearly (jury selection, challenges, opening statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial begins with impaneling a jury; attorneys challenge prospective jurors (for cause or peremptorily). The state's attorney makes the opening statement, then the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting trials, explain jury selection methods, peremptory-challenge limits, and summarize opening themes so readers grasp trial dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain witness examinations and courtroom sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses undergo direct examination, cross-examination, possible redirect and recross; the state presents witnesses first, then the defense, followed by summations and jury deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the order of witness testimony and highlight key cross-examinations or legal objections that shape credibility and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report verdict outcomes and post-verdict remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'not guilty' verdict frees the accused; a 'guilty' verdict allows appeal requests, motions to dismiss, or retrial. If the jury cannot agree, the judge may continue deliberations or order a new trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include verdict result, possibility of appeal, and any immediate post-verdict motions or sentencing actions in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the coroner's role and relation to preliminary examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The coroner inquires into deaths that might be criminal, may summon witnesses, and in some states the coroner's inquest replaces the preliminary examination; in others it merely justifies an arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting suspicious deaths, clarify whether an inquest or preliminary hearing has occurred and what authority the coroner exercised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report when prosecutors enter nolle prosequi (charges dropped)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prosecuting attorney decides that all or part of the accusations should be dropped, he requests the magistrate to enter a 'nolle prosequi' finding, removing the accusations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain 'nolle prosequi' to readers and report its practical effect — charges dismissed — and any stated reasons if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain change-of-venue motions and grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused person may request a 'change of venue' on grounds such as flaming community prejudice which would prevent selecting a truly impartial jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report venue-change motions and the prosecutor's/defense's arguments about community prejudice and impartiality, since they affect trial fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain extradition and 'continuous pursuit' exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extradition is used when an accused has left the state; governors hear arguments and decide. Some states have compacts allowing officers to arrest across state lines on 'continuous pursuit' without formal extradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an out-of-state arrest or transfer occurs, explain whether it was by extradition request or under a continuous-pursuit compact and what that implies procedurally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe habeas corpus as a remedy for illegal detention
rubrics_metrics.description: A writ of habeas corpus requires the custodian to bring the prisoner before a court and show cause for continued confinement; if not shown, the court releases the prisoner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use habeas-corpus filings to report allegations of unlawful detention and explain their immediate legal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain civil-case pleadings and pretrial motions (complaint, demurrer, motion, plea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil cases often begin with a 'complaint' or 'declaration' by the plaintiff and may include a 'praecipe' or summons. The defendant may present a 'demurrer', 'motion', or 'plea' to clarify, narrow, or deny the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report what the pleadings and motions seek to resolve (e.g., dismissal, narrowing issues) so readers understand what dispute the trial will actually address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain remedies in civil cases and execution of judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court decides for the defendant, expenses may be awarded; if for the plaintiff, appropriate relief and possibly costs. If a judgment debtor fails to pay, the winning party may obtain an 'execution' to seize and sell property at auction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting civil judgments, state the remedy awarded and any enforcement steps (levy, execution) expected to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain equity suits and injunction types (temporary, permanent, preliminary/restraining orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity asks the court to order action or cessation of action; injunctions may be temporary (to preserve status quo until trial) or permanent. A preliminary injunction or restraining order is an emergency finding issued before defense arguments are heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between temporary restraining orders, preliminary injunctions, and permanent injunctions in coverage, and report their immediate effects on parties' conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover special courts and probate procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain matters (estates, guardianship, adoptions) are handled in special 'probate' courts. Procedures include appointment of executor/administrator, issuance of letters testamentary, appraisal and inventory, creditor notices, final account and discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In estate-related reporting, explain the probate steps and terminology (executor vs administrator, intestate) and report notices, inventories, and distributions that affect third parties and creditors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn local court nomenclature and chain of courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Court names and jurisdiction vary locally (justice, police magistrate, county, circuit/district/superior, appellate, supreme); courts are ranked according to seriousness of cases they may handle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should learn local court names and jurisdictional limits to accurately describe which court handled a matter and its authority; explain appeals structure when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain federal-court jurisdiction and the federal court ladder
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal system begins with the district court (original jurisdiction in many federal matters), then circuit courts of appeals (appellate), and the United States Supreme Court (largely appellate). Federal courts have exclusive jurisdiction in areas like copyright, patents, admiralty, bankruptcy, and federal-law prosecutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In federal-case coverage, state why the federal forum is proper or exclusive, and explain the appeals path (district → circuit → Supreme Court) when reporting outcomes or pending appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reporter habits for the courts beat
rubrics_metrics.description: Seasoned reporter's aids: buy a one-volume dictionary of legal terms, study Latin grammar for legal terms, cultivate the clerk of courts by asking many questions, and don't hesitate to ask judges for explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt these learning and relationship-building practices: carry reference books for on-the-spot clarity, build sources (clerks) for quick interpretation, and seek judges' guidance to ensure accurate reporting of complex legal points.
